notes: The written form has “his eyes”; the reading tradition has “his eye.” Both picture an appetite that wealth cannot satisfy.

The succession story leaves several relationships uncertain: whose kingdom it is, who was born poor, and which young man replaces whom. The draft keeps those uncertainties rather than supplying a complete history.
This edition follows Hebrew numbering here. This verse is 5:1 in many English Bibles; the following chapter has nineteen verses.
vocabulary: The book’s recurring image for what is fleeting, elusive, or frustrating to grasp.

notes: “Messenger” can also mean “angel.” The setting involves an unfulfilled vow, but the messenger’s exact role is unstated.

This compressed verse is difficult. It may describe the king’s dependence on cultivated land or the advantage of a king who serves agriculture; it follows a description of officials watching officials.
The verb can suggest that God keeps this person occupied with gladness, or answers through gladness. The verse does not erase the injustices described earlier.
vocabulary: A promise made to God. The warning concerns fulfilling what one has freely promised.

notes: The comparison with a stillborn child is deliberately stark. It concerns frustrated enjoyment and rest, and is not softened into a general comment about disappointment.
The Hebrew word can mean “words” or “things.” Either reading continues the question of what multiplication actually gains a person.
vocabulary: Literally “life” or “soul” here: the desiring self, pictured as wandering beyond what the eyes can see.

notes: The text says “too righteous,” not “self-righteous.” Its warning about destructive excess stands alongside the warning against wickedness and the call to fear God.
These are Qohelet’s gender-specific judgments within his account of searching. The translation preserves both their severity and his repeated limits on what he has found.
vocabulary: The Hebrew designation used for the book’s speaking teacher; it is related to gathering or an assembly.

notes: The same Hebrew word can mean “wind,” “breath,” or “spirit.” The line joins lack of control over it with lack of control over death.
The Hebrew text used here says “were forgotten.” “Were praised,” found in some translations, reflects a different textual reading.
The conviction that fearing God brings good is followed by an observation that righteous and wicked people receive the opposite of what their conduct would suggest. The tension remains in the text.
vocabulary: What God does in the world, which the speaker says people cannot fully discover despite their efforts.

sections.10: Justice and what cannot be explained

notes: The reading tradition has “joined”; the written consonants suggest “chosen.” The draft follows the reading tradition.
The speaker describes the dead as excluded from what happens “under the sun.” The translation leaves his stark claims intact without adding a systematic account of life after death.
vocabulary: The realm of the dead in the poem’s Hebrew vocabulary.

sections.1: A shared fate and life’s gifts

notes: The last clause may mean that the fool reveals his own folly to everyone, or calls everyone else a fool.
The compressed final clause connects wisdom with successful action; its exact syntax is uncertain. The blunt-iron comparison remains visible.
“Boy” may emphasize youth, inexperience, or low status. The contrast is with a king of noble birth in the next verse.
vocabulary: Enslaved people. The reversal of riding and walking concerns status in the speaker’s social world.

notes: Bread sent across water and shares given to seven or eight are open images. They have been understood in terms of generosity, trade, and spreading risk; the translation does not replace the images with one explanation.
“Wind” can also be “breath” or “spirit.” The line can join two unknown processes, or speak of breath entering the child whose bones form in the womb.
vocabulary: A rare expression associated with youth; it may evoke early life or dark hair.

notes: The aging and death imagery is left as poetry. Identifying every household object or figure with one body part would make the translation more certain than the text.
The phrase may refer to collected sayings or to masters of collections. “One shepherd” is not explicitly identified in the verse.
Literally, “this is all of the human.” It can express everyone’s obligation or what makes up a whole human life.
vocabulary: The recurring opening image returns at the close of Qohelet’s words, before the book’s concluding assessment.
